Read About Da Nang

A river town the Cham built a religion around, the French ran as a port, the Americans turned into a battlefield, and Vietnam turned into a beach resort — in that order, on the same six miles of coast.

A city with someone else's name on the ruins

Before it was Da Nang, this stretch of coast was called Cửa Hàn — the mouth of the Han — by the Vietnamese court that eventually absorbed it. Before that, it belonged to Champa, an Indianized Hindu and Buddhist kingdom that ran the central Vietnamese coast for the better part of a thousand years and never built a single unified capital the way its neighbors did. Champa moved its political centers as fortunes shifted: Indrapura, near modern Dong Duong about 50 kilometers south, held power from roughly 875 to 982 AD; Singhapura, at what's now the village of Tra Kieu, came earlier. What stayed constant through all of it was My Son, 40 kilometers inland — not a capital but a sanctuary, the religious heart of Champa for over a thousand years, where more than seventy brick temple towers were raised to Shiva across successive dynasties.

The Museum of Cham Sculpture in downtown Da Nang exists because of a specific act of French curiosity. In 1919, colonial archaeologists gathered the sandstone and terracotta carvings being pulled out of Champa sites across the region — dancing apsaras, guardian lions, lingam altars — and built a museum to hold them, a decade before the French colonial state that commissioned it even had a name for the country it was studying. It remains the only collection of its kind anywhere, because nowhere else concentrated this much Cham stonework in one place, and because so much of what wasn't collected there was later lost.

What the Americans did to the sanctuary

My Son survived Champa's decline, French rule, and the first Indochina war essentially intact. It did not survive 1969. Believing — correctly, as it turned out — that Viet Cong forces were using the ruins for cover, American B-52s carpet-bombed the site over the course of about a week, reducing roughly two-thirds of its structures to rubble. The main tower, group A1, had been considered one of the finest examples of Cham architecture anywhere; it is now a low pile of brick. Craters from the raid are still visible between the surviving groups, softened by seventy years of grass and, in the rainy season, standing water. UNESCO inscribed what remains as a World Heritage Site in 1999, precisely because so little of it remains.

Hoi An, 40 minutes from My Son by road, was never touched. The two sites sit less than an hour apart and tell opposite stories about the same war.

Hoi An's survival wasn't an accident of geography so much as of relevance — it had already been eclipsed as a port by the deepening of the Han River channel decades earlier, and by the 1960s it simply wasn't a military target the way My Son's suspected tunnel network was. What's left is a trading town that peaked in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, when Chinese, Japanese, Dutch, and Portuguese merchants all kept warehouses along its river frontage, and then went quiet enough, for long enough, that nobody bothered to modernize it. The Japanese Covered Bridge, built around 1593 to link the Chinese and Japanese merchant quarters, is one of the few surviving pieces of physical infrastructure anywhere in Vietnam built by a resident Japanese trading community — a group that existed in Hoi An for barely a century before Japan sealed its borders and cut them off entirely.

China Beach, and the war Da Nang actually fought

On March 8, 1965, roughly 3,500 US Marines waded ashore at My Khe Beach — the stretch of sand the hotel now sits on — in the first official deployment of American combat troops to Vietnam. Da Nang Air Base, just inland, grew into one of the busiest airfields on Earth by the war's peak, handling more sorties in some years than any airport in the world, military or civilian. The beach itself became a designated rest-and-recreation site for American and Australian troops, who nicknamed it China Beach after the sea it fronted — not for any Chinese presence, just informal wartime shorthand for the South China Sea. A television drama borrowed the name two decades later and made it internationally famous for reasons that had nothing to do with the actual beach.

The mountain at the northern tip of the peninsula tells a quieter version of the same story. Son Tra — what the Americans called Monkey Mountain, for the actual troops of macaques living on it — held a joint Air Force and Marine radar and signals-intelligence station from 1962 until the facility closed in 1971, tracking North Vietnamese radio traffic and controlling fighter cover over the whole of I Corps. Today the peninsula is a protected nature reserve and the last significant stronghold of the red-shanked douc langur, an endangered primate so visually strange — a face like porcelain, a coat striped in five colors — that National Geographic has run multiple features on the population living within sight of where the radar towers once stood.

A hill station built for people escaping the heat, twice

Ba Na Hills has been a retreat from Da Nang's climate for over a century, though the people escaping it have changed completely. In 1919, the same year the Cham museum opened, French colonial administrators built a hill station at nearly 1,500 meters — more than 200 villas, a hospital, tennis courts, switchback roads — so that colonists could spend the hot season at temperatures twenty degrees cooler than the coast. Decades of war and neglect afterward let the jungle reclaim almost all of it; by the 1990s there was little left to see. Sun Group began redeveloping the site in 2007, and the version that exists now — a cable car system, a French-village theme park, and since 2018 the Golden Bridge, held aloft by two enormous weathered hands — draws more visitors in a single day than the original hill station saw in a season.

The bridges, and what they replaced

Da Nang crosses the Han River nine times, more than any Vietnamese city its size, and the bridges are treated less as infrastructure than as civic performance. Dragon Bridge, completed in 2013, is shaped like a dragon in mid-flight and breathes actual fire and water from its head on weekend nights — a fact that surprises visitors who assume it's a figure of speech until they're standing on the riverbank at 9pm on a Saturday. It replaced a much plainer crossing, and it arrived at almost the exact moment Da Nang itself was being repositioned: from a war-scarred port city that most of the country associated with the military, into the beach resort now competing directly with Phuket and Bali for the same travelers.

That repositioning happened fast, inside two decades, and it's still visible in the seams — a Han riverfront of glass towers a few minutes' drive from fishing boats that haven't changed their routine in generations, a coastline of five-star resorts backing directly onto villages where three generations still share one house. Nothing about that contrast has been smoothed over yet, which is part of what makes the city interesting to move through right now, before it finishes deciding what it wants to be.

The road north, over the pass

Leaving Da Nang by train, as this trip does on its last day, means crossing the Hai Van Pass — the Ocean Cloud Pass — a serrated mountain spur that drops almost to the water and has functioned as the traditional boundary between Vietnam's central and northern climate zones for longer than anyone kept written records of it. French engineers spent decades in the early twentieth century blasting a rail line through it, tunnel by tunnel, along a route so scenic that Vietnamese and international rail enthusiasts still rank it among the great train journeys of Southeast Asia. On the far side is Hue, capital of the Nguyen dynasty for 143 years and the closest thing Vietnam has to its own Forbidden City — walled, moated, and built in direct imitation of Beijing's, by an empire that spent a century and a half insisting it was Beijing's equal.
